statement: Popular sources commonly gloss Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka as "Great Spirit," implying a singular personified deity comparable to the Christian God. Named ethnographic sourcing (James R. Walker, fieldwork 1896-1914 at Pine Ridge, published as Lakota Belief and Ritual, ed. Raymond J. DeMallie and Elaine A. Jahner, University of Nebraska Press, 1980/1991) records Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka as "Tobtob Kin" ("the four times four" — sixteen distinct sacred entities/aspects, e.g. Wi the sun, Hanwi the moon, Škáŋ the sky/motion, Tate the wind, Uŋčí Makȟá the earth, Wakíŋyaŋ the Thunder-being) simultaneously described as "one" — a unified-multiplicity, pantheistic/panentheistic structure, not an anthropomorphic single deity. William K. Powers, Oglala Religion (University of Nebraska Press, 1977/1982), corroborates this general structure. Specialist consensus judges "Great Mystery" or "Great Sacred" a more accurate rendering than "Great Spirit," which is flagged as a post-contact, missionary-influenced reading layered onto an older, more diffuse framing.

sources.citation: Walker, James R. Lakota Belief and Ritual. Ed. Raymond J. DeMallie and Elaine A. Jahner. Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 1980/1991.
sources.author: James R. Walker

does_not_demonstrate: That Wakȟáŋ Tȟáŋka is accurately rendered by the popular "Great Spirit" gloss, which imports a monotheistic personification the sixteen-aspect Tobtob Kin structure does not carry
